answers.why: Limited resources vs unlimited wants: the basic economic problem.

Getting the most output or benefit from given resources, with no waste.

prompts.prompt: Name a leakage or an injection in the circular flow of income

answers.why: Leakage: income not spent, which flows to financial markets. Its matching injection is investment.
Leakage: income taken by government. Its matching injection is government spending.
Leakage: spending that flows out to other countries. Its matching injection is exports.

Injection: government expenditure, financed partly by tax revenue.

prompts.prompt: Name something a PPC diagram can show

answers.why: Moving along the curve means giving up some of one good to get more of the other.
Points outside the curve are unattainable with current resources and technology.
Growth is shown by the curve shifting outward, or by a point moving toward the curve.
Society has to pick one combination (one point) on the curve.

Any point ON the curve: you can't make more of one good without making less of the other.
A point inside moving to the curve, using idle resources. The curve itself doesn't move.
The whole curve shifts outward because of more or better resources or technology.
Points outside the curve can't be produced with today's resources and technology.
Bowed-out curve: resources are specialised, so each extra unit costs more of the other good.
Straight-line PPC: resources are equally suited to both goods.
A fall in production possibilities, e.g. after a war or natural disaster destroys resources.

prompts.prompt: Name an economist, school of thought or big idea from the schools-of-thought lesson

Marx's idea that the value of goods comes from the labour used to make them.

prompts.prompt: Name a basic economic question or a type of economic system

Basic question 2: which methods and resources should be used?

Markets plus government intervention. Every real economy is mixed to some degree.

prompts.prompt: Name a non-price determinant of demand

answers.why: Higher income shifts D right for normal goods and left for inferior goods.
Fashion, advertising or health news in favour of a good shift D right.
A substitute gets dearer, so buyers switch to this good and D shifts right.
A complement gets dearer, so both goods are bought less and D shifts left.
More buyers (population growth, tourism) shift D right.
If buyers expect prices to rise soon, they buy more now and D shifts right.
Seasonal or weather changes shift tastes, e.g. umbrella demand in the monsoon.

prompts.prompt: Name a determinant of supply (think STORES)

answers.why: T in STORES: better technology cuts costs, so S shifts right.
R: dearer wages, materials or energy make production less profitable, so S shifts left.
S: a tax raises the cost per unit, so S shifts up/left by the tax.
S: a subsidy lowers firms' costs, so S shifts down/right.
S (size): more firms in the market shift S right, and firms leaving shift it left.
E: firms expecting higher future prices may hold back supply now.
O: making one good also makes another (beef and leather), so their supply moves together.
O: the same resources could make either good. A better price for one pulls resources from the other.
Weather or natural disasters (drought, floods) suddenly shift supply, especially for farm goods.

prompts.prompt: Name an event that shifts DEMAND to the right

answers.why: For a normal good, higher income means more demand at every price.
Advertising changes tastes in the good's favour.

alias: rise in price of a substitute
answers.why: Buyers switch away from the dearer rival (Pepsi dearer, so demand for Coke rises).

alias: fall in price of a complement
answers.why: Cheaper printers mean more demand for ink, since the goods are used together.
More consumers in the market.
Buyers expecting a higher price later buy more now.
For an INFERIOR good (instant noodles), lower income raises demand.
Tourists add buyers, e.g. for hotel rooms and taxis.
A study praising a food shifts tastes toward it.

prompts.prompt: Name an event that shifts SUPPLY to the left

answers.why: The tax per unit raises costs, so S shifts up by the tax.
Labour costs rise, which is the R (resource costs) in STORES.
Dearer inputs mean less is profitable to supply at every price.
A supply shock: farm output falls whatever the price.
Fuel and electricity are inputs too, so S shifts left.
Taking away a subsidy raises firms' costs again.
Fewer sellers means less supply at every price.
A flood or earthquake destroys capacity.
Farmers switch fields to the now dearer crop, so supply of this crop falls.
Firms hold stock back now to sell later at the higher price.

prompts.prompt: Name a key term from market equilibrium and the price mechanism

answers.why: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so the market clears.
Excess demand: below the equilibrium price, Qd > Qs, so price gets bid up.
Excess supply: above the equilibrium price, Qs > Qd, so sellers cut the price.
The area above the price and below D: what buyers were willing to pay minus what they paid.
The area below the price and above S: the price received minus the lowest price firms would accept.
Prices carry information. A rising price tells producers more is wanted (Uber surge).
Higher prices motivate firms to supply more (surge pay pulls drivers on the road).
A rising price decides who gets scarce goods: those willing and able to pay.
At equilibrium, MB = MC (D = MB, S = MC). Society gets the goods it values most.
Consumer + producer surplus. It is maximised at the competitive equilibrium.
After a demand shift, price rises and Qs extends along S. Supply itself does not shift.

prompts.prompt: Name a determinant of price elasticity of demand (think HINTS)

answers.why: S in HINTS: more and closer substitutes make it easy to switch, so demand is more elastic.
N: essentials (insulin, Daraprim) are bought whatever the price, so demand is inelastic.
T: buyers can't switch at first. Over time they find alternatives, so PED rises in the long run.
I: a big share of income (cars) makes demand elastic. A tiny share (salt) makes it inelastic.
H: addictive or habit-forming goods (cigarettes) keep being bought, so demand is inelastic.

alias: how broadly the good is defined
answers.why: One brand has many substitutes (elastic). A whole category like 'all biscuits' is inelastic.

prompts.prompt: Name a determinant of PES (think TRICS), or a time period used to analyse it

answers.why: T in TRICS: supply is inelastic in the short run because of time lags, and more elastic over time.
C: unused machines and workers let output rise quickly, so supply is elastic.
I: firms holding stock can release it fast, so supply is elastic. Perishables can't be stored.
S (substitute factors): mobile inputs can switch to the good whose price rose, so supply is elastic.
R: if marginal cost rises slowly, supply is elastic. If it rises fast (deep oil wells), inelastic.
Some inputs are fixed (no new factory yet), so PES is low.
All inputs can change (new farms and factories), so PES is higher.
So short that output can't change at all: PES = 0, a vertical supply curve.

prompts.prompt: Name a degree of PED, or the diagram shape that shows it

answers.why: |PED| > 1: quantity demanded changes proportionately MORE than price.
0 < |PED| < 1: quantity demanded changes proportionately LESS than price.

PED = 0: quantity doesn't change at all when price changes.
PED = infinity: any price rise above P* loses every buyer.
Shows PED = 0 (perfectly inelastic): quantity never moves.
Shows PED = infinity (perfectly elastic).
HL: on a straight-line D, PED = 1 exactly at the midpoint.
The bowed curve where P x Q is the same everywhere, so PED = 1 at every point.

prompts.prompt: Name a good likely to have price-INELASTIC demand

answers.why: Few substitutes in the short run and needed for commuting, so demand is inelastic.

A tiny share of income, so a price rise is barely noticed.
Habit-forming, and governments tax it for revenue because demand is inelastic.
A staple food (necessity) with few substitutes in many diets.
An essential with no easy substitute in the short run.
An essential with no substitute.
Primary commodity: an essential input with few substitutes, so PED is low.
The class case: price jumped from $13.50 to $750, but it's life-saving with no substitute.
Cheap medicine: a tiny income share and a necessity, so PED is low.

prompts.prompt: Name a good likely to have price-ELASTIC demand

answers.why: Not essential and easy to postpone, so buyers react strongly to price.
Other brands sit on the same shelf. One brand is elastic, but all biscuits aren't.
Easy to cut back on, so a price rise means fewer dinners out.
A large share of income, so a price rise noticeably cuts purchasing power.
Not essential, and lots of alternative destinations.
Coke vs Pepsi: close substitutes mean high PED for a single brand.
Not a necessity, with many rival brands.
Leisure spending with many alternatives (streaming, other outings).
Many cafes nearby. In the class example, a 10% price cut raised cups sold 20% (PED = -2).
Practice-paper case: a 10% price cut raised sales 25% (PED = 2.5), so TR rose.

prompts.prompt: Name an inferior good (negative YED)

Demand falls as income rises because people switch to fresh food.

prompts.prompt: Name a luxury good or service (YED > 1)

Drill: incomes +8% with YED 2.5 means demand +20%.
Spending on it rises faster than income.
Branded fashion is income-elastic.

A slide example: demand changes proportionately more than income.
Supermarkets stock more of it in a boom, because it's a luxury.

prompts.prompt: Name a necessity good (0 < YED < 1)

answers.why: You eat only a little more rice when richer. Drill: income +10%, rice +3%, so YED = 0.3.
A class slide example: demand rises much more slowly than income.
Basic food: demand barely rises with income.
A staple. The Engel curve example shows bread changing type as income rises.
An everyday essential with low YED.
Basic hygiene: demand rises slowly as income rises.
Essential: use rises with income, but less than proportionately.
Food (primary sector) has a low YED, which is why that sector shrinks as countries grow.

prompts.prompt: Name a way firms or governments use PED

answers.why: When PED < 1, a price rise increases total revenue.
Governments tax cigarettes and alcohol: quantity barely falls, so revenue is large.

Peak holiday airfares and surge pricing: demand is inelastic at that moment.
With inelastic demand, a firm can pass a cost rise on to buyers without losing many sales.
The less elastic side bears more of the tax. If PED < PES, consumers pay most.

answers.why: PED side: food and fuel are essentials, so people keep buying when prices rise.

PED side: the cotton in a shirt is a tiny part of its cost, so buyers barely react.

prompts.prompt: Name a feature of PED along a straight-line demand curve (HL)

answers.why: Same slope everywhere, but PED runs from infinity down to 0. Slope is not elasticity.
PED = 1 exactly halfway along the line.
Above the midpoint: high P, low Q, so %ΔQ is big and %ΔP small. PED > 1.
Below the midpoint: PED < 1.
Total revenue peaks where PED = 1. Price changes either way lower TR.
Slope uses absolute changes, PED uses % changes. That's why they differ.
Marginal revenue: the extra revenue from one more unit sold.
MR hits zero at the midpoint quantity, the same point where TR peaks.
For a linear D, MR starts at the same price intercept and is twice as steep.
As Q approaches 0 (where D meets the price axis), PED approaches infinity.
Where D meets the quantity axis (P = 0), PED = 0.
The demand curve is also the average revenue curve, because AR = TR ÷ Q = price.

answers.why: Two panels, same price rise. The flat curve loses a lot of quantity, the steep one little.
A vertical D labelled PED = 0.
A horizontal D at P*, labelled PED = infinity.
Shade the revenue lost (A) and gained (B) when price changes. The bigger box decides TR.
S from the Q-axis = inelastic, from the P-axis = elastic, through the origin = PES 1.
Income on the vertical axis. Shows luxury, then necessity, then inferior as income rises.
A rectangular hyperbola. Equal rectangles show constant TR.
HL: PED from infinity to 0 along D, MR twice as steep, and a TR hill peaking at the midpoint.
S shifts up by the tax. Consumer and producer burdens are split at the old price.
Momentary (vertical), short run (steep) and long run (shallow) through one point.
HL: steep D and S. A supply shock causes a big price swing for a small quantity change.

prompts.prompt: Name a term linked to why YED matters for firms and the economy (HL)

Rising incomes: luxury sales jump the most.

prompts.prompt: Name a type of good classified by its YED or XED

answers.why: YED > 0: demand rises as income rises.

XED negative: goods used together (petrol and SUVs).

prompts.prompt: Name a letter of CLASPP, the evaluation toolkit

answers.why: Who wins and who loses, with numbers if possible. Use this one every time.
What the theory takes for granted (ceteris paribus, constant PED). Use this one every time too.
Effects change over time. PED for petrol is low now but rises as people switch.
A weighed, conditional verdict that answers the question, not a summary.

prompts.prompt: Name a stakeholder to weigh in a market or policy evaluation

answers.why: Pay higher prices or gain cheaper goods. Under a tax on inelastic demand they bear most of it.

Jobs and wages depend on what happens to output.

Listed in the class feedback: when one good gets dearer, sellers of substitutes win.

People outside the deal, e.g. the health system bearing smoking costs.
A sustainability angle: who pays later for today's choices?

answers.why: Start by defining the key terms in the question, word-perfect.

answers.why: Give the precise meaning of a term. Usually 2 marks.
Give a detailed account with reasons or causes. Usually needs a diagram in Economics.
Weigh strengths and limitations and reach a supported judgement. The 15-mark term.

cards.back: The study of choices leading to the best possible use of scarce resources to best satisfy unlimited human needs and wants; a social science.
Resources are limited/finite AND cannot produce everything humans need and want (unlimited wants) — both halves required.
The value of the next best alternative that is given up/sacrificed when a choice is made.
A good that is not scarce and therefore has zero opportunity cost and no price (e.g. air, sunlight).
A model showing all combinations of the maximum output of two goods an economy can produce, given fixed resources and technology, with full and efficient employment of resources.
Represents unemployed or inefficiently used resources — output could increase without new resources.
Represents a currently unattainable combination given existing resources and technology.
Movement from a point inside the PPC toward the curve, achieved by using previously idle/unemployed resources; the curve itself does not move.
An outward shift of the entire PPC, caused by more/better resources or improved technology; also called potential growth.
Each additional unit of one good costs progressively more of the other good, because resources are not equally suited to producing both — shown by a bowed-out (concave) PPC.
An outward or inward shift that favours one good's axis more than the other, caused by a change specific to producing that good (e.g. new technology in only one industry).

cards.front: Zero opportunity cost (from an interior point)
cards.back: Moving from a point INSIDE the PPC to a point ON it uses previously idle/unemployed resources, so nothing else has to be sacrificed — distinct from a movement ALONG the curve, which does carry an opportunity cost.
Latin for "other things being equal/held constant"; the assumption that all other relevant variables are held unchanged so the effect of one variable can be isolated and analysed.
A testable, verifiable "is" statement about the world; can be proven false and still be positive (e.g. a wrong statistic is still a positive statement).
A value judgment or prescriptive statement, typically containing "should," "ought," or "too much/little."
Fairness in the distribution of resources or outcomes — a normative, value-based concept.
A model showing the flow of income, expenditure, and factors of production between households and firms (and, in the five-sector version, financial markets, government, and the foreign sector).
Income that flows OUT of the circular flow instead of being spent on domestic output — savings, taxes, and imports.
Spending that flows INTO the circular flow from outside the household-firm loop — investment, government spending, and exports.
Causes national income/output to FALL, because more money is exiting the circular flow than is being injected back in.
Causes national income/output to RISE, because more money is being injected into the circular flow than is leaking out.

The value of everything produced (output) equals total income earned (from selling that output) equals total expenditure (spent buying it) — three equivalent ways of measuring the same national income.

Scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence, intervention — the organizing concepts of the whole DP Economics course; each IA commentary must use a different one.
The critique that real decision-makers have limited information, time, and cognitive ability, so they cannot make perfectly rational decisions as classical theory assumes.
18th-century idea that self-interest in free markets, guided by an "invisible hand," serves society without government intervention; foundation of classical economics.
View, following the Great Depression, that markets do not always self-correct and government must intervene (e.g. spending) to revive demand in a recession.
Field incorporating psychology into economics, showing real people do not always act as perfectly rational, utility-maximizing agents.

cards.front: Factors of production and their rewards
cards.back: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest, entrepreneurship earns profit.
What (and how much) to produce, how to produce it, and for whom to produce it.
Savings and investment (financial markets); taxes and government spending (government); imports and exports (foreign sector).
Units of the other good given up ÷ units gained. E.g. giving up 500,000 chocolate bars for 3,000 watches = about 167 bars per watch.
Planned: the state owns resources and central planners allocate them. Mixed: markets plus government intervention. All real economies are mixed.
The quantities of a good or service that consumers are willing and able to buy at different possible prices over a given time period.
As price rises, quantity demanded falls (and vice versa), ceteris paribus: an inverse relationship, so D slopes down.
The quantities of a good or service that firms are willing and able to produce and sell at different possible prices over a given time period.
As price rises, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus: a positive relationship, because higher prices give firms an incentive to produce more.
Own price change = movement ALONG the curve (change in quantity demanded/supplied). Non-price determinant = SHIFT of the whole curve (change in demand/supply).
Subsidies and taxes, Technology, Other related goods (joint/competitive supply), Resource costs, Expectations, Size/number of firms.
Income (normal/inferior), tastes and preferences, prices of substitutes and complements, expectations, number of consumers.
Joint: making one good also makes another (beef and leather). Competitive: the same resources make either good (a field for wheat OR corn).
Shortage (excess demand): price below equilibrium, Qd > Qs, so price is bid up. Surplus (excess supply): price above equilibrium, Qs > Qd, so price falls.

cards.front: Three functions of the price mechanism
cards.back: Signalling (prices carry information), incentive (higher prices motivate more supply), rationing (scarce goods go to those willing and able to pay).
The benefit consumers get from paying less than the most they were willing to pay: the area below D and above the price.
The benefit producers get from selling above the lowest price they would accept: the area above S and below the price.
Producing what society values most, where marginal benefit = marginal cost (D = MB, S = MC). Reached at competitive equilibrium, where social surplus is maximised.

cards.front: The #1 trap after a demand shift
cards.back: Price rises and QUANTITY SUPPLIED extends along S. Supply does not shift because of price. Only a non-price determinant shifts a curve.
A measure of the responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good or service to a change in its price.
%Δ quantity demanded ÷ %Δ price. The value is negative (law of demand) and read as an absolute value.
(new − old) ÷ old × 100. Always divide by the OLD (original) value. Elasticities have no units and no % sign.
A change in price leads to a proportionately larger change in quantity demanded: |PED| > 1.
A change in price leads to a proportionately smaller change in quantity demanded: PED between 0 and 1.

cards.front: Unit elastic, perfectly inelastic, perfectly elastic
cards.back: Unit: PED = 1, equal % changes, TR unchanged. Perfectly inelastic: PED = 0, vertical D. Perfectly elastic: PED = ∞, horizontal D.
Habits, Income share, Necessity, Time, Substitutes (number and closeness). Give one determinant with a full chain, not a list.
Inelastic: raise price and TR rises. Elastic: cut price and TR rises. Unit elastic: TR unchanged. TR = P × Q.
When price falls, area A = revenue lost on existing units and area B = revenue gained on extra units. If B > A, TR rises (elastic demand).

cards.front: PED along a linear demand curve (HL)
cards.back: Elastic above the midpoint, PED = 1 at the midpoint (TR max, MR = 0), inelastic below. Slope is constant but PED isn't.
Price went from $13.50 to $750 a tablet (5,500%). Life-saving, no close substitutes, small share of income: extremely inelastic, so revenue jumped.
A measure of the responsiveness of demand to a change in (real) income. YED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔY. Keep the sign.
Normal: YED > 0. Necessity: 0 < YED < 1. Luxury: YED > 1. Inferior: YED < 0 (instant noodles, canned food, second-hand clothes).
Income (vertical) against quantity (horizontal). Flat zone = luxury, steep zone = necessity, bending back = inferior. A good can change type as income rises.
Luxuries swing most with the cycle, necessities are least affected, and inferior goods are counter-cyclical (they sell more in recessions).
Primary goods have 0 < YED < 1, manufactured goods YED > 1 and services even higher. As incomes rise the tertiary sector grows fastest.
A measure of the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price. PES = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP. Always ≥ 0.
Time, Rate at which costs increase, Inventory (ability to store), Capacity (spare), Substitute factors (factor mobility).
Straight S from the Q-axis: PES < 1. From the P-axis: PES > 1. Through the origin: PES = 1. Vertical: 0. Horizontal: ∞.
Momentary period: output fixed (PES = 0). Short run: some inputs fixed (low PES). Long run: all inputs variable (higher PES).

cards.front: Why primary commodities have low PED
cards.back: They're necessities with few substitutes (food, oil), and often a small share of the final product's cost.

cards.front: Why primary commodities have low PES
cards.back: Long growing times, perishable (can't store), land fixed (no spare capacity), immobile factors, and costs rise fast in extraction.

cards.front: Low PED + low PES for commodities
cards.back: A supply shock (drought or bumper harvest) causes big price swings and a small quantity change, so farm incomes are volatile.
%ΔQd of A ÷ %ΔP of B. Positive = substitutes, negative = complements (used together), about 0 = unrelated.
A raw material produced in the primary sector (agriculture, fishing, forestry, mining), e.g. coffee, wheat, copper, crude oil.
The tax shifts S up by the tax per unit. The less elastic side bears more of it: with inelastic demand, consumers pay most.
Define, Diagram, Explain, Example (DEED). For a 15-marker add Evaluation (CLASPP) and a conditional conclusion.
Conclusions, Long vs short run, Assumptions, Stakeholders, Priorities, Pros/cons. Use at least 3, always including Stakeholders and Assumptions.
Ruler, title, axes with units, every curve labelled, intersections marked, dotted lines to both axes, areas labelled, exact values, arrows (dynamic).

cards.front: Writing a calculation for full marks
cards.back: Line 1: both % changes with numbers. Line 2: formula with numbers in. Line 3: answer (2 dp, sign) plus a word, e.g. '−0.50, inelastic'.
If an early figure is wrong but you use it correctly later, you still get the later marks, but only if your working is shown.
Theory fully explained in context, terms used throughout, diagrams included AND fully explained, effective and balanced evaluation, supported judgement.
Explain: a cause-and-effect chain, no judgement needed. Evaluate: weigh both sides and reach a conditional judgement. Don't evaluate when asked to explain.
Two halves: what kind of thing it is plus the precise condition, and the value range if it has one. Never define with an example alone.

quiz.q: A point INSIDE the PPC shows…
quiz.explain: Inside = idle or misused resources. ON the curve = productively efficient. OUTSIDE = unattainable for now.

quiz.q: Moving from A to B along a PPC, an economy gains 3,000 watches and gives up 500,000 chocolate bars. What is the opportunity cost of one watch?
quiz.explain: Opportunity cost = amount given up ÷ units gained = 500,000 ÷ 3,000 ≈ 167 bars per watch.

quiz.q: Which is a NORMATIVE statement?
choices: A higher minimum wage will raise unemployment
The government should raise the minimum wage
quiz.explain: 'Should' is a value judgement. A wrong statistic is still positive, because it can be tested.

quiz.q: Which list contains only LEAKAGES from the circular flow?
quiz.explain: Leakages leave the household-firm loop: S, T, M. Injections come in: I, G, X.

quiz.q: A bowed-out (concave) PPC shows…
quiz.explain: Resources are specialised, so each extra unit of one good costs more and more of the other.

quiz.q: Which school argued governments should spend to fight a recession?
quiz.explain: Keynes, after the Great Depression: markets don't always self-correct, so government spending revives demand.

quiz.q: The price of a good rises. On a diagram this is shown as…
choices: A shift of demand to the left
A shift of supply to the right
A shift of demand to the right
A movement along the demand curve
quiz.explain: A change in the good's own price moves you along the curve: a change in quantity demanded, not in demand.

quiz.q: Demand for hotel rooms shifts right. What happens next, ceteris paribus?
choices: Price rises and quantity supplied extends along S
quiz.explain: Supply never shifts because of price. The higher price causes a movement along S (Qs rises).

quiz.q: Which is NOT a determinant of supply in STORES?
quiz.explain: Income is a determinant of DEMAND. STORES: Subsidies/taxes, Technology, Other related goods, Resource costs, Expectations, Size/number of firms.

quiz.q: At a price BELOW equilibrium there is…
choices: A shortage, so price is bid up
quiz.explain: Below Pe, Qd > Qs (excess demand). Buyers bid the price up until Qd = Qs.

quiz.q: Uber surge pay pulling more drivers onto the road is an example of the price mechanism's…
quiz.explain: Higher prices raise profit per ride, which motivates more supply: the incentive function.

quiz.q: Consumer surplus is the area…
choices: Below the price and above supply
Between S and D to the right of equilibrium
Above the price and below demand
quiz.explain: What buyers were willing to pay minus what they paid: above P, below D.

quiz.q: Beef and leather are an example of…
quiz.explain: Producing beef automatically produces leather, so their supplies move together.

quiz.q: Coffee falls from $2.00 to $1.80 and cups sold rise from 100 to 120. PED is…
quiz.explain: %ΔQd = +20%, %ΔP = −10%. PED = 20 ÷ −10 = −2, so |2| > 1 and demand is elastic. TR rises from $200 to $216.

quiz.q: Chai rises from ₹20 to ₹22 and cups sold fall from 100 to 95. What happens to total revenue?
quiz.explain: %ΔQd = −5%, %ΔP = +10%, so PED = −0.5. TR goes from ₹2,000 to ₹2,090.

quiz.q: 800 units are demanded at $20 and PED = −0.4. Price rises to $40. The new quantity demanded is…
PED = −4 and sales rose 10%. What price change caused it?
quiz.explain: %ΔP = %ΔQd ÷ PED = 10 ÷ −4 = −2.5%, a price cut.

quiz.q: A price goes from ₹120 to ₹100. The percentage change is…
quiz.explain: Divide by the OLD value: (100 − 120) ÷ 120 × 100 = −16.7%.

quiz.q: Real incomes rise 10% and bus rides fall from 40 to 36. YED is…
quiz.explain: %ΔQd = −10%, %ΔY = +10%, so YED = −1.0. The negative sign means an inferior good. Keep the sign!

quiz.q: Incomes rise 8% and the YED for flights is 2.5. Demand for flights…
quiz.explain: %ΔQd = YED × %ΔY = 2.5 × 8 = +20%. YED > 1, so flights are a luxury.

quiz.q: Household income rises from ₹50,000 to ₹55,000 and rice bought rises from 10 kg to 10.3 kg. Rice is…
quiz.explain: %ΔQd = +3%, %ΔY = +10%, so YED = 0.3. Between 0 and 1 means a normal good and a necessity.

quiz.q: Avocado prices rise from $2.00 to $2.50 and quantity supplied rises from 1,000 to 1,100 tonnes. PES is…
quiz.explain: %ΔQs = +10%, %ΔP = +25%, so PES = 0.4. Trees take years to mature (Time in TRICS).

quiz.q: World coffee price falls from $4.00 to $3.20 and supply falls from 500,000 to 490,000 tonnes. PES is…
quiz.explain: %ΔQs = −2%, %ΔP = −20%, so PES = 0.1: very inelastic, typical of a primary commodity.

quiz.q: A sugary drink rises from 50 to 58 and sales fall from 40m to 36.8m litres. PED is…
Coffee's price rises 10% and demand for tea rises 5%. XED is…
quiz.explain: XED = +5 ÷ +10 = +0.5. Positive means substitutes (weak ones, since it's below 1).

quiz.q: Which is a determinant of PES, not PED?
quiz.explain: Spare capacity (the C in TRICS) is about sellers' ability to raise output. The others are HINTS demand-side reasons.

quiz.q: On a straight-line demand curve, total revenue is maximised…
choices: Where the curve meets the price axis
Where the curve meets the quantity axis
At the midpoint, where PED = 1 and MR = 0
quiz.explain: TR rises while demand is elastic and falls once it's inelastic, so it peaks at the midpoint where PED = 1.

quiz.q: A straight supply line that starts on the QUANTITY axis has…
quiz.explain: Inelastic S cuts the Q-axis, elastic S cuts the P-axis, and any line through the origin has PES = 1. (A class slide swaps these.)

quiz.q: Why do governments tax cigarettes to raise revenue?
choices: Demand is price inelastic, so quantity barely falls
quiz.explain: Inelastic demand (habit) means sales fall only a little, so tax × quantity stays large. But it cuts smoking only a little.

quiz.q: Which is the BEST reason primary commodities have low PED?
choices: Crops take a long time to grow
They are necessities with few substitutes
quiz.explain: PED reasons are about buyers. Growing time, storage and fixed land are PES (supply-side) reasons.

quiz.q: Inferior goods are described as counter-cyclical because…
choices: They sell more in recessions as incomes fall
quiz.explain: YED < 0, so when incomes fall in a recession, demand for them rises.

quiz.q: For a 'Define' question worth 2 marks, which answer scores 2/2 for 'inferior good'?
choices: A good with negative YED: as income rises, demand for it falls
quiz.explain: Two halves: what it is (negative YED) plus the condition (demand falls as income rises). An example alone scores 0.

quiz.q: Which CLASPP angles should you use in EVERY evaluation?
quiz.explain: The class rule: at least three angles, always including Stakeholders and Assumptions, plus one of your choice.

quiz.q: A calculation answer with the right number but NO working usually earns…
quiz.explain: Working (both % changes plus the formula) is the method mark. The answer alone gets 1 of 2.

quiz.q: What most often caps a 15-mark essay in the middle band?
quiz.explain: Top bands need diagrams included and fully explained AND balanced evaluation with a supported judgement.

quiz.q: An 'Explain…' 10-marker needs…
choices: Definitions, a narrated diagram, an explained chain and an example, with no evaluation needed
quiz.explain: Explain = Define, Diagram, Explain, Example. Evaluation earns nothing extra under 'explain' and wastes time.

quiz.q: Which conclusion is most likely to reach the top band?
choices: On balance the tax raises revenue now, but cuts consumption only in the long run, provided substitutes are taxed too.
In conclusion, there are pros and cons.
quiz.explain: A contingent judgement: it weighs both sides, answers the question and names the conditions.
